Accepted edges glow green, rejected cycle-forming edges glow red, and the redundant structure of the full graph becomes legible through what must be left out. The artifact makes efficiency feel like subtraction. | themes: algorithms misc | complexity: beginner | tags: graph_theory minimum_spanning_tree kruskal prim union_find optimization algorithm | identity: Pure F as optimization: the graph's cheapest connected backbone emerges by stripping away redundant cycles. Necessity becomes visible edge by edge. algorithm_type ("kruskal" vs "prim") — Kruskal processes edges globally by weight (greedy on edges), Prim grows locally from a root (greedy on vertices) — same result, different experience the minimum spanning tree is the cheapest way to keep everyone connected — every edge in it is necessary, and removing any one disconnects the network Kruskal's (sort edges by weight, Union-Find to reject cycles) or Prim's (grow tree from starting vertex, always add cheapest crossing edge) — both find the minimum-weight spanning tree to watch the cheapest skeleton of a network assemble edge by edge — green edges accepted, red edges rejected for creating cycle

description: Read a network as hierarchy, community, and circulation at once. It complements the explicit flow algorithms by building intuition for why some nodes matter more than others.

description: Two CSG primitives combined with the union operator. Visualizes A union B as a single composite solid.
card: name: csg union demo | family: boolean surfaces | description: Two CSG primitives combined with the union operator. Visualizes A union B as a single composite solid. | themes: boolean surfaces sieve 2026 05 13 | category: boolean_surfaces | complexity: intermediate | tags: csg boolean union F_order | identity: sphere_offset — how far the sphere sits from the box. Far apart = barely fused; overlapping = one blob. The overlap is where union does its work. Union is the generous operator. It keeps everything either shape claims. A ∪ B — the union operator. Two CSG primitives (box + sphere) fused into one seamless solid; where they overlap, no seam survives. To show that joining is not stacking. The union is a single skin around two volumes, not two objects merely touching.

description: Two CSG primitives with intersection operator. Only the overlap survives.
card: name: csg intersection demo | family: boolean surfaces | description: Two CSG primitives with intersection operator. Only the overlap survives. | themes: boolean surfaces sieve 2026 05 13 | category: boolean_surfaces | complexity: intermediate | tags: csg boolean intersection F_order | identity: sphere_offset — controls how much the primitives overlap. Small overlap = a sliver; full overlap = nearly a whole primitive; no overlap = nothing at all. Intersection is the shape of consensus. What both shapes agree on is always less than either alone. A ∩ B — the intersection operator. Only the volume present in BOTH primitives survives; the result is a lens where the two shapes agree. To show that agreement has a shape, and that it is always smaller than either party brought to it.

description: A box with a sphere subtracted. The operator that makes cavities and openings.
card: name: csg difference demo | family: boolean surfaces | description: A box with a sphere subtracted. The operator that makes cavities and openings. | themes: boolean surfaces sieve 2026 05 13 | category: boolean_surfaces | complexity: intermediate | tags: csg boolean difference F_order | identity: sphere_offset — where the bite lands. Center = a clean internal void; edge = an open notch that breaks the silhouette. To make a room, subtract a void from a solid. Architecture is difference. A − B — the difference operator. A solid box minus an invisible sphere; only the sphere's negative space survives, biting a cavity into the box. To reveal that absence is constructive. The hole is not missing material — it is the operator's product.

description: Workbench holding all three CSG operators side by side. The introduction artifact for the csg-compose catalyst affordance.
card: name: csg compose workbench | family: boolean surfaces | description: Workbench holding all three CSG operators side by side. The introduction artifact for the csg-compose catalyst affordance. | themes: boolean surfaces sieve 2026 05 13 | category: boolean_surfaces | complexity: intermediate | tags: csg catalyst_affordance workbench | identity: preset_spacing — how far apart the three demonstrations sit. Too close and the operators blur together; too far and the comparison between them is lost. Three operators, one algebra. Composition is a choice — keep all, keep the shared, or take away. A workbench holding all three CSG operators side by side — union, intersection, difference — applied to the same box+sphere pair, each labeled by symbol. To let the player meet the whole composition algebra at once and pick an operator by hand with the catalyst bracelet.

description: A solid wall with three openings cut through it. Architecture as Boolean composition.
card: name: csg architecture cavity | family: boolean surfaces | description: A solid wall with three openings cut through it. Architecture as Boolean composition. | themes: boolean surfaces sieve 2026 05 13 | category: boolean_surfaces | complexity: intermediate | tags: csg architecture boolean wall | identity: wall_size against the opening sizes — the ratio of solid to void. Too little solid and the wall stops reading as a wall; too little void and it stops being architecture. Every architectural cavity is a difference. A room is a wall that has been subtracted from. A thick wall with three openings — doorway, circular porthole, arched window — each a CSG subtraction from the same solid. Architecture as Boolean difference. To turn the difference operator into a habitable space the player can walk through, not merely observe.

description: Watch a sequence of weak learners focus on what the previous ones got wrong. Each decision stump is simple — a single threshold on one axis. card: name: adaboost | family: machinelearning | description: Watch a sequence of weak learners focus on what the previous ones got wrong. Each decision stump is simple — a single threshold on one axis. But AdaBoost weights misclassified points heavier, so each new stump specializes on the hard cases. Points that keep getting misclassified visually grow larger. The ensemble decision boundary gets progressively more sophisticated from trivially simple components. | themes: machinelearning | category: machinelearning | complexity: intermediate | tags: machinelearning boosting adaboost ensemble weak-learner decision-stump classification weighting | identity: Lambda-tuning — the alpha weight per stump is the lambda that tunes how much each weak learner contributes. The ensemble is a weighted sum where lambda encodes earned trust. n_rounds — how many weak learners to add. Too few = underfitting. Too many = overfitting. The sweet spot is where the weighted vote stabilizes. AdaBoost is a conversation between failure and focus. Each mistake makes the next learner pay more attention to what was missed. w(i) *= exp(alpha * err_i). Points that the last stump got wrong get heavier. The next stump focuses on the hard cases. Watch a sequence of weak learners (stumps) each specialize on what the previous one failed. The ensemble gets smarter by remembering its mistakes.

description: A motorized crank mechanism combining three joint types into one machine. Watch how continuous rotation becomes reciprocating translation through the geometry of constraint.

To see a web of springs breathe — wind perturbing it, colors shifting with tension, the whole system finding equilibrium and losing it again.

description: Position-based Verlet integration — the workhorse of game physics and molecular dynamics. Instead of tracking velocity explicitly, it infers motion from the difference between current and previous positions. This makes it naturally stable, time-reversible, and beautifully simple: x_new = 2x_current - x_old + a·dt².
card: name: verlet integration | family: physics simulation | description: Position-based Verlet integration — the workhorse of game physics and molecular dynamics. Instead of tracking velocity explicitly, it infers motion from the difference between current and previous positions. This makes it naturally stable, time-reversible, and beautifully simple: x_new = 2x_current - x_old + a·dt². | themes: numerical methods verlet position based stability | category: physics | complexity: intermediate | tags: verlet integration position_based stable time_reversible molecular_dynamics game_physics | identity: F-computation — the most stable integration method works by forgetting velocity. Position history encodes all the information. Simpler representation, better stability. dt — at small dt, Euler and Verlet look the same. At large dt, Euler escapes, Verlet stays. The most stable integration method is the one that forgot to track the thing everyone assumed was essential. x(t+dt) = 2x(t) - x(t-dt) + a(t)*dt². No velocity. Positions remember. To show that forgetting velocity makes physics better. To make the learner SEE energy conservation.

description: A cellular automaton that grows fracture networks from invisible stress. Hidden state is hostile state — once managers' fields are pinned to a Label3D, the world has receipts, and the player can finally find out what the curriculum thinks it's doing. read(EcosystemManager) + read(HazardManager) + read(CatalystCapabilityManager) → three columns of Label3D + scrolling log. To make the invisible game state legible — soft-stage progression is hidden in autoload singletons until this panel pins it to a wall and lets you read where you are in the curriculum.

Hidden state becomes survivable once you can rewind it — the curriculum that can only advance is a trap, but a slider that lets you go back is a learning aid. slider(sequence_order) + button(force_advance_to) + button(befriend_hazard) + button(reset) → write to EcosystemManager + HazardManager + CatalystCapabilityManager. A VR control surface for the curriculum's hidden state machine. To turn the soft_stages.json progression from a thing that happens to you into a thing you can scrub through — letting playtesters jump to seq 12 to feel "ecology turned on" without grinding 11 levels.

description: Six StaticBody3D walls (floor, ceiling, +X, -X, +Z) enclose a 5x5x3 m room; the -Z wall is two side panels + a lintel leaving a 1.2x2.2 m entrance you walk through. An invisible doorway curtain on the ball-only collision layer keeps thrown balls inside while letting the player pass. Balls are RigidBody3D with a bouncy physics material (engine bounces; we visualise). Each ball caches its pre-contact velocity every physics frame; on wall contact it recovers the incident d, looks up the wall's inward normal n̂, computes r = d - 2(d.n̂)n̂, and spawns a ~1.5 s fading d/n̂/r arrow cluster + live formula at the hit point, verifying r against the post-bounce velocity. Fading per-ball trails via ImmediateMesh line strips. A grab-throw ball rack (primary VR) plus an optional ANGLE/FORCE/FIRE console; on desktop/headless the console auto-fires every ~3 s so captures show live bounces. Sweeping it IS the lesson: small n hides every difference (all bars short), large n is where the choice between O(n) and O(n²) is the difference between instant and never. an algorithm is not one thing — it is a curve. Two solutions that agree on every small case can disagree about whether the universe has enough time. Complexity is the shape of that disagreement. the COMPLEXITY RACE — six bars, one per Big-O class (O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n²), O(2ⁿ)), that grow as the input size n sweeps up.
